song-dynastie-erfindungen#summary: The first recipe for gunpowder is recorded in Song China in 1044; the compass, paper money, and movable type follow in the same century.
song-dynastie-erfindungen#text: The Song dynasty, founded in 960, ruled an economically flourishing China with cities of a million people such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou. In 1044 the military manual Wujing Zongyao described for the first time mixtures of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal for fire arrows and bombs; fire lances and explosive bombs followed in the 12th century. In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo recorded how a magnetized needle points south, and Chinese seafarers soon used the compass for navigation. The state issued the world's first paper money, Bi Sheng invented movable type, and iron production reached quantities that Europe did not match again until the 18th century.
cahokia-mississippi-kultur#title: Cahokia, center of the Mississippian culture
cahokia-mississippi-kultur#summary: On the Mississippi the largest settlement in North America north of Mexico arises.
cahokia-mississippi-kultur#text: Opposite present-day St. Louis, Cahokia grew around 1050 into a city of probably 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants. Its basis was maize farming in the fertile river floodplain. More than a hundred earthen mounds carried temples, elite houses and graves; the largest, Monks Mound, is about 30 meters high and the largest earthwork in North America. Circles of wooden posts probably served as solar calendars. Cahokia shaped the Mississippian culture throughout the Southeast, but lost inhabitants from about 1200 and was largely abandoned by 1350.
schlacht-bei-hastings#summary: Duke William of Normandy defeats the Anglo-Saxon king Harold and conquers England.
schlacht-bei-hastings#text: After the death of the childless king Edward the Confessor, William claimed the English throne, which Harold Godwinson had, however, already taken. On 14 October 1066 the armies met near Hastings; Harold fell in the fighting, and William had himself crowned at Westminster at Christmas. The Norman Conquest brought to England a French-speaking nobility, castles of stone, the feudal system, and a tight administration, recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086. The Bayeux Tapestry tells the events across seventy meters of cloth.
al-bakri-beschreibt-ghana#title: Al-Bakri describes the empire of Ghana
al-bakri-beschreibt-ghana#summary: The geographer al-Bakri in Córdoba portrays the West African gold empire of Ghana and its court.
al-bakri-beschreibt-ghana#text: The empire of Ghana, called Wagadu by its inhabitants, the Soninke, lay in the border region of the present-day states of Mauritania and Mali. It controlled the trade between the goldfields in the south and the caravans from North Africa that brought salt and goods across the Sahara. The scholar al-Bakri, who never went there himself, collected merchants' reports in Córdoba and in 1068 described a capital in two parts: a town of Muslim traders with twelve mosques and the royal town with sacred groves. The king ruled with great splendor and levied duties on every load of salt. His account is one of the most important sources on the first great empire of West Africa.
schlacht-von-manzikert#summary: Sultan Alp Arslan defeats the Byzantine army and takes Emperor Romanos IV prisoner; Anatolia becomes Turkish and Islamic.
schlacht-von-manzikert#text: The Seljuks, a Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia, had adopted Sunni Islam, taken Baghdad in 1055, and placed the Abbasid caliph under their protection; from then on their ruler bore the title of sultan. On 26 August 1071 Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes faced Alp Arslan's army at Manzikert in eastern Anatolia, was defeated by the cavalry tactics of the Turks, and was taken captive. Alp Arslan released him for a ransom, but civil wars broke out in Byzantium, and Turkish tribes advanced almost unhindered into Asia Minor, where the Sultanate of Rum arose with its capital at Konya. The Byzantine emperor's appeal to the pope for help was one of the reasons for the First Crusade in 1096.
gang-nach-canossa#title: The Investiture Controversy and the road to Canossa
gang-nach-canossa#summary: King Henry IV stands as a penitent before the castle of Canossa and asks Pope Gregory VII to lift his excommunication.
gang-nach-canossa#text: Pope Gregory VII had forbidden rulers to install bishops in office with ring and staff, because he wanted to free the church from secular power. When Henry IV responded in 1076 by declaring the pope deposed, Gregory pronounced the ban on the king and released his subjects from their oath of loyalty. Pressed by the princes, Henry crossed the Alps in winter and waited for three days in January 1077 in penitential dress before the castle of Canossa, until Gregory received him back into the church. The conflict continued for decades and was ended only in 1122 by a compromise in the Concordat of Worms.
kanem-herrscher-hume-wird-muslim#title: The ruler of Kanem converts to Islam
kanem-herrscher-hume-wird-muslim#summary: With King Hume, a ruler of the empire of Kanem on Lake Chad becomes a Muslim for the first time.
kanem-herrscher-hume-wird-muslim#text: The empire of Kanem lay northeast of Lake Chad and lived from trade along the caravan route to Fezzan and Libya, on which mainly slaves, ivory and horses were traded. According to tradition, King Hume converted to Islam in the late 11th century and founded the Sayfawa dynasty. This ruling family reigned until 1846 and thus ranks among the longest-lasting dynasties in world history. In the 14th century the kings moved their seat to Bornu, west of the lake, which is why historians speak of the empire of Kanem-Bornu. Several rulers made the pilgrimage to Mecca and maintained relations as far as Egypt.
gruendung-der-universitaet-bologna#title: Founding of the University of Bologna
gruendung-der-universitaet-bologna#summa: Europe's first university grows out of the law schools of Bologna; Paris and Oxford follow in the 12th century.
gruendung-der-universitaet-bologna#text: In Bologna scholars such as Irnerius had specialized in the rediscovered Roman law of Justinian and attracted students from all over Europe. Around 1088 these students joined together in corporations that hired professors and regulated teaching; the word university originally denoted this community of teachers and learners. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa placed the scholars under his protection in 1155, and the popes gave their degrees validity throughout Christendom. By 1500 there were around 70 universities, among them Paris, Oxford, Salamanca, Prague, Vienna, and Heidelberg.
erster-kreuzzug#title: The First Crusade and the capture of Jerusalem
erster-kreuzzug#summary: At the pope's call, knights from all over Europe march to the Holy Land and capture Jerusalem.
erster-kreuzzug#text: At the Synod of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II called for help for the Byzantine Christians and for the liberation of the holy sites from Muslim rule. Tens of thousands answered the call, among them knights under Godfrey of Bouillon and Raymond of Toulouse. After a costly march through Asia Minor and the siege of Antioch, the crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and carried out a massacre of the population. They founded several crusader states, which held out for almost two centuries; six more major crusades followed.
beginn-der-gotik#title: The beginning of Gothic architecture at Saint-Denis
beginn-der-gotik#summary: Abbot Suger has a light-filled choir built near Paris and with it establishes the style of the Gothic cathedrals.
beginn-der-gotik#text: In 1140 Abbot Suger began rebuilding the abbey church of Saint-Denis, the burial place of the French kings, combining pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows into a new whole. Because the weight of the vaults was carried from outside by buttresses, the walls could be made thin and the light, which for Suger was an image of God, could enter unhindered. Within a few decades the cathedrals of Chartres, Paris, Reims, and Amiens were built on this model, and in 1248 construction of Cologne Cathedral began. With their towers, sculptures, and rose windows, the Gothic cathedrals were the tallest buildings of their time and an expression of the pride of the growing cities.
angkor-wat#summary: The Khmer build the largest temple complex in the world in present-day Cambodia.
angkor-wat#text: In the first half of the 12th century, King Suryavarman II had Angkor Wat built as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu and as his own tomb. Surrounded by moats, the complex with its five towers reproduces Mount Meru, the world mountain of Hindu cosmology, and is decorated with reliefs kilometers long. The Khmer empire then ruled large parts of Southeast Asia and supplied its capital by means of an ingenious canal system. Angkor Wat later became a Buddhist sanctuary and is today the national symbol of Cambodia.
ibn-ruschd-erklaert-aristoteles#title: Ibn Rushd explains Aristotle in Córdoba
ibn-ruschd-erklaert-aristoteles#summary: At the request of the Almohad caliph, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd begins his commentaries on Aristotle, which change the thought of Europe.
ibn-ruschd-erklaert-aristoteles#text: Around 1169 the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf commissioned the scholar Ibn Rushd of Córdoba to explain the difficult writings of Aristotle. Over the following decades Ibn Rushd wrote commentaries on almost all the works of the Greek philosopher and, in a treatise of his own, defended the compatibility of reason and revelation against the criticism of the theologian al-Ghazali. In 1195 he fell out of favor for a time because of his philosophy and had to go into exile. His commentaries were translated into Latin and Hebrew as early as the 13th century; at the University of Paris he was known simply as the Commentator, and Thomas Aquinas engaged with him intensively.
saladin-erobert-jerusalem-zurueck#summar: After his victory at Hattin, Saladin takes the city again almost nine decades after the First Crusade.
saladin-erobert-jerusalem-zurueck#text: Saladin had united Egypt and Syria under his rule and called for war against the crusader states. On 4 July 1187, at the Horns of Hattin, he destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which was cut off from water in the summer heat. On 2 October Jerusalem capitulated; unlike the crusaders in 1099, Saladin spared the inhabitants and let them leave on payment of a ransom. The loss of the city set off the Third Crusade, in which Richard the Lionheart did win back Acre, but Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands.
minamoto-no-yoritomo-wird-shogun#summary: The victor of the Genpei War receives the title of shogun from the emperor and establishes Japan's first warrior government in Kamakura.
minamoto-no-yoritomo-wird-shogun#text: In the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 the warrior clan of the Minamoto defeated their rivals, the Taira. Their leader Yoritomo set up his government not at the imperial court in Kyoto but in Kamakura in eastern Japan, and in 1192 received the title of shogun. This began a period of almost 700 years in which military governments ruled the country while the emperor performed mainly ceremonial duties. After Yoritomo's death the family of his widow Hōjō Masako took over the leadership as regents.
grosssimbabwe#summary: In southern Africa the ancestors of the Shona build a stone city that lives from the gold trade with the Swahili coast.
grosssimbabwe#text: Between the 11th and 15th centuries a city of up to 18,000 inhabitants arose on the plateau of present-day Zimbabwe, its rulers controlling cattle herds and gold deposits. Its walls of carefully layered granite blocks, set without mortar, reach eleven meters in height; the Great Enclosure with its conical tower is the largest precolonial structure south of the Sahara. Finds of Chinese porcelain, Persian ceramics, and Arab coins show that gold and ivory were traded through ports such as Kilwa and Sofala as far as India and China. The city was abandoned around 1450; colonial researchers long disputed the African origin of the buildings, which today give the state of Zimbabwe its name and its emblem.
koepfe-von-ife#summary: In the sacred Yoruba city of Ife, naturalistic heads of copper alloy and terracotta of great artistry are created.
koepfe-von-ife#text: In Yoruba tradition, Ife in the southwest of present-day Nigeria is the place where the world was created and the place of origin of their royal families. Between the 12th and 15th centuries artists there made life-size heads of copper alloys using the lost-wax technique, as well as of fired clay. The faces are so lifelike that European researchers such as Leo Frobenius at first refused to believe they were African works. They probably depicted kings and dignitaries and were used in rituals. The art of Ife influenced the later casters in the kingdom of Benin.
felsenkirchen-von-lalibela#summary: Under King Lalibela, eleven churches are carved entirely out of the living rock in the Ethiopian highlands.
felsenkirchen-von-lalibela#text: Lalibela belonged to the Zagwe dynasty, which ruled Christian Ethiopia after the decline of Aksum. Around 1200, in the town later named after him, eleven churches were created that were not built of masonry but carved downwards out of the volcanic rock. The most famous, Bete Giyorgis, has the ground plan of a cross and stands in a deep pit. According to tradition, the complex was meant to represent a new Jerusalem after pilgrimage to the Holy Land had become difficult. The churches are still the destination of countless pilgrims and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
taino-haeuptlingstuemer-in-der-karibik#t: The Taíno chiefdoms of the Caribbean
taino-haeuptlingstuemer-in-der-karibik#s: On the Greater Antilles the Taíno develop a society with caciques, ball courts and ancestral figures.
taino-haeuptlingstuemer-in-der-karibik#t: The ancestors of the Taíno had migrated from South America along the island chain of the Lesser Antilles. By around 1200 a society with hereditary chiefs, the caciques, among them women, had developed on Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Cuba and Jamaica. The Taíno grew cassava on heaped-up earth mounds, traveled between the islands in large dugout canoes and played a ball game on plazas lined with stones, the bateyes. They venerated spirits and ancestors in figures called zemís. Words such as canoe, hammock, hurricane and tobacco come from their language.
dschingis-khan-einigt-die-mongolen#summa: Temüjin is proclaimed ruler of all the Mongol tribes and begins to build a world empire.
dschingis-khan-einigt-die-mongolen#text: At an assembly of the tribes on the Onon River in 1206, Temüjin received the title Genghis Khan, which means roughly oceanic or universal ruler. He organized the Mongols into units of ten, a hundred, and a thousand warriors, introduced a law code, and promoted men by achievement rather than by birth. His mounted archers conquered northern China, Central Asia, and Persia; his successors extended the empire as far as Eastern Europe and southern China. Despite the brutality of their warfare, the Pax Mongolica later secured trade along the Silk Road.
gruendung-des-delhi-sultanats#summary: After the death of his master Muhammad of Ghor, the commander Qutb ud-Din Aibak makes himself independent in Delhi and founds the first lasting Muslim state in northern India.
gruendung-des-delhi-sultanats#text: Qutb ud-Din Aibak had risen as a military slave and had conquered large parts of northern India for Muhammad of Ghor. He had already begun the Quwwat al-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar minaret in Delhi; after his master's death in 1206 he ruled as an independent sovereign. The sultanate was ruled in turn by five dynasties and repelled several Mongol attacks in the 13th and 14th centuries. From 1236 to 1240 a woman, Radiyya, even ruled as sultan. In 1526 Babur defeated the last sultan at Panipat.
magna-carta#summary: English barons force King John to acknowledge their rights in a charter.
magna-carta#text: King John Lackland had turned the nobility against him through lost wars in France and heavy levies. On 15 June 1215, in the meadow of Runnymede, he had to set his seal to Magna Carta, which laid down among other things that no free man may be imprisoned without lawful judgment and that no tax may be levied without the consent of the council. The charter at first applied only to the nobility and was soon annulled again, yet it was confirmed over and over and became a symbol of the ruler's subjection to the law.
sundiata-schlacht-von-kirina#title: Sundiata wins at Kirina and founds Mali
sundiata-schlacht-von-kirina#summary: The Mande prince Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso king Sumanguru and lays the foundation of the Mali Empire.
sundiata-schlacht-von-kirina#text: After the decline of Ghana, the Sosso king Sumanguru Kante had subjugated the lands on the upper Niger. Sundiata Keita, a Malinke prince, rallied the Mande peoples against him and defeated him around 1235 in the battle of Kirina. He then became the founder of the Mali Empire, which in the following decades expanded from the Atlantic to the bend of the Niger and controlled the goldfields of Bambuk and Bure. His life is known above all through the epic of Sundiata, which griots still perform today. Rules for the coexistence of the clans, known in oral tradition as the Kurukan Fuga charter, were also traced back to him.
mongolensturm-in-osteuropa#title: The Mongol invasion of Eastern Europe
mongolensturm-in-osteuropa#summary: Mongol armies under Batu conquer the Russian principalities, destroy Kyiv and win victories in 1241 at Legnica and on the Sajó river in Hungary.
mongolensturm-in-osteuropa#text: From 1237 the Mongols under Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, attacked the divided principalities of Rus and took one city after another. Kyiv fell in December 1240, and in April 1241 Mongol armies defeated a Silesian-Polish force at Legnica and the Hungarian army at Mohi on the Sajó. After the death of the Great Khan Ögedei they withdrew unexpectedly in 1242. On the Volga Batu founded the Golden Horde, to which the Russian princes paid tribute for more than two centuries.
mongolen-zerstoeren-bagdad#summary: Hülegü's army captures and plunders Baghdad and brings the Abbasid caliphate to an end.
mongolen-zerstoeren-bagdad#text: The Mongol prince Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, marched on Baghdad with an enormous army after its caliph al-Mustasim had refused to submit. After a short siege the city fell in February 1258; tens of thousands of inhabitants were killed, palaces, mosques, and libraries were destroyed, and the caliph was executed. The end of the Abbasid caliphate and the devastation of the irrigation system in Mesopotamia struck the Islamic world hard. In 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in Palestine; a few decades later the Mongol rulers of Persia themselves adopted Islam.
yekuno-amlak-salomonische-dynastie#title: Beginning of the Solomonic dynasty in Ethiopia
yekuno-amlak-salomonische-dynastie#summa: Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe kings and founds a dynasty that traces its origin back to King Solomon.
yekuno-amlak-salomonische-dynastie#text: Yekuno Amlak, a lord from the province of Amhara, ended the rule of the Zagwe dynasty in 1270. His successors justified their power with the legend that they descended from Menelik, the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. In the 14th century this story was written down at length in the Kebra Nagast, the Book of the Glory of Kings. The Solomonic dynasty ruled, with interruptions, until 1974, when Emperor Haile Selassie was overthrown. It bound the monarchy closely to the Ethiopian church.
kublai-khan-gruendet-die-yuan-dynastie#t: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
kublai-khan-gruendet-die-yuan-dynastie#s: The Mongol ruler Kublai Khan proclaims a dynasty on the Chinese model and by 1279 unites all of China under Mongol rule.
kublai-khan-gruendet-die-yuan-dynastie#t: Kublai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, had made himself Great Khan in 1260 after a war with his brother. In 1271 he gave his rule in China the Chinese dynastic name Yuan and made Dadu, present-day Beijing, his capital. By 1279 he had conquered the Southern Song empire and reunited China for the first time in centuries. The Mongols divided the population into ranked classes in which the southern Chinese stood at the very bottom. The Yuan promoted trade and paper money but were overthrown by uprisings in 1368.
marco-polos-reise-nach-china#summary: The young Venetian travels with his father and uncle along the Silk Road to the court of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan.
marco-polos-reise-nach-china#text: In 1271 the seventeen-year-old Marco Polo set out from Venice with his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo, and after almost four years reached the residence of Kublai Khan in China. By his own account he spent some seventeen years in the service of the Great Khan and traveled through large parts of East Asia before returning by sea in 1295. In Genoese captivity he dictated his experiences, which became known as Il Milione. The account of paper money, coal, and huge cities shaped the European picture of Asia and later inspired Columbus.
mongolenstuerme-auf-japan#summary: Two invasion fleets sent by Kublai Khan fail against the Japanese defences and violent storms, which are revered in Japan as kamikaze, the divine wind.
mongolenstuerme-auf-japan#text: After Japan had refused to submit, a Mongol-Korean army landed in Hakata Bay on Kyūshū in 1274 but withdrew after fighting and a storm. The government in Kamakura then had a defensive wall built along the coast. In 1281 an even larger fleet came from Korea and southern China and, after weeks of fighting, was largely destroyed by a typhoon. The Japanese saw this as the protection of the gods. However, the cost of the defence weakened the Kamakura shogunate, which fell in 1333.
gruendung-des-osmanischen-reiches#summar: The Turkish prince Osman makes himself independent in northwestern Anatolia and founds a dynasty that will rule for six centuries.
gruendung-des-osmanischen-reiches#text: After the collapse of the Sultanate of Rum, numerous Turkish principalities arose in Anatolia. On the border with Byzantium, Osman I led warriors who saw themselves as fighters for the faith, and step by step he conquered Byzantine cities. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it the first capital; in 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe. Within 150 years they had conquered the Balkans and Constantinople and had become the leading power of the Islamic world, one that lasted until 1922.
bluete-von-kilwa#title: The flourishing of the Swahili city of Kilwa
bluete-von-kilwa#summary: Through the gold trade, the island city of Kilwa on the coast of present-day Tanzania becomes the richest trading city in East Africa.
bluete-von-kilwa#text: Kilwa Kisiwani controlled the trade in gold from the Zimbabwe plateau, which reached the coast through the port of Sofala. Its sultans minted their own copper coins and in the early 14th century had the Great Mosque enlarged and the palace of Husuni Kubwa built. Ibn Battuta visited the city around 1331 and praised it as one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Merchants from Arabia, Persia and India brought cloth, beads and Chinese porcelain. In 1505 the Portuguese conquered and plundered Kilwa, and the city never recovered.
mansa-musas-pilgerreise#summary: The king of the Mali empire crosses the Sahara to Mecca with an enormous caravan and tons of gold.
mansa-musas-pilgerreise#text: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali empire, which with the gold mines of the western Sudan and the trading cities of Timbuktu and Gao was among the richest states in the world. On his pilgrimage in 1324 he was accompanied, according to contemporary reports, by thousands of people and camels loaded with gold, which he gave away so freely in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. On the way back he brought scholars and master builders with him and had mosques and schools built in Timbuktu. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a nugget of gold as the ruler of West Africa.
reisen-des-ibn-battuta#summary: A Moroccan jurist crosses the entire Islamic world from West Africa to China in almost thirty years.
reisen-des-ibn-battuta#text: Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in 1325 on the pilgrimage to Mecca and then traveled on: to East Africa, Anatolia, the court of the Golden Horde, and India, where he served for years as a judge to the sultan of Delhi, and on to the Maldives, Sumatra, and China. After his return he also visited al-Andalus and the Mali empire in West Africa. In all he covered around 120,000 kilometers, far more than Marco Polo. His travel account, the Rihla, is one of the most important sources on society, trade, and everyday life in the Islamic world of the 14th century.
gruendung-tenochtitlans#title: Founding of Tenochtitlan by the Aztecs
gruendung-tenochtitlans#summary: The Mexica found the city that becomes the capital of the Aztec empire on an island in Lake Texcoco.
gruendung-tenochtitlans#text: According to tradition, the Mexica settled where they saw an eagle on a cactus, as their god Huitzilopochtli had foretold; that image adorns the flag of Mexico today. Through causeways, floating gardens, and canals, the island settlement grew into a city of more than 200,000 inhabitants, with huge temple pyramids and markets. From 1428 Tenochtitlan, in a triple alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, ruled large parts of Mexico and demanded tribute and captives for human sacrifice. In 1521 the Spaniards under Cortés conquered the city; Mexico City arose on its ruins.
timbuktu-gelehrtenzentrum#title: Timbuktu becomes a center of trade and scholarship
timbuktu-gelehrtenzentrum#summary: Under the Mali empire, the caravan city on the Niger develops into a center of the gold trade and of Islamic scholarship.
timbuktu-gelehrtenzentrum#text: Timbuktu had come into being around 1100 as a camping place of Tuareg nomads on the edge of the Sahara, where caravans carrying salt from the desert met boats from the Niger carrying gold, ivory, and slaves. After his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa brought back the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili in 1325, who built the great Djinguereber Mosque out of mud brick; at the Sankoré Mosque and in private houses, schools arose in which scholars from North Africa and Egypt taught law, grammar, astronomy, and medicine. In the 15th and 16th centuries, under the Songhai empire, Timbuktu was one of the most important centers of learning in Africa, with thousands of students and a lively trade in manuscripts. Tens of thousands of these manuscripts survive to this day and refute the prejudice that Africa south of the Sahara had no written culture.
eroberung-von-bursa#summary: After a long siege the Ottomans take the Byzantine city of Bursa and make it their first capital.
eroberung-von-bursa#text: Osman's warriors had blockaded Bursa at the foot of Mount Uludağ from fortresses for years until the starving city surrendered to his son Orhan in 1326. Osman died around this time and was buried in Bursa. Orhan made the city his capital, had mosques, baths and caravanserais built, and soon also conquered Nicaea (1331) and Nicomedia (1337). Bursa became a centre of the silk trade between Persia and Europe and remained the burial place of the early sultans.
gruendung-von-vijayanagara#summary: The brothers Harihara and Bukka found a Hindu empire in southern India whose capital becomes one of the largest cities in the world.
gruendung-von-vijayanagara#text: According to tradition, around 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the city of Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, on the Tungabhadra river. The empire soon dominated all of southern India and was in constant rivalry with the Muslim sultanates of the Deccan. Under King Krishnadevaraya it reached its height in the early 16th century; Portuguese visitors described the capital as magnificent and as large as Rome. In 1565 its army was defeated at Talikota by an alliance of the sultanates, and the capital was plundered. Its ruins at Hampi are now a World Heritage Site.
hundertjaehriger-krieg#summary: England and France struggle for more than a century over the French throne and the territories in western France.
hundertjaehriger-krieg#text: The war began when the English king Edward III, as the grandson of a French king, claimed the crown of France. English longbowmen won at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356, and Agincourt in 1415, and for a time France was close to falling apart. In 1429 Joan of Arc turned the tide by relieving Orléans and led the Dauphin to his coronation at Reims. With the battle of Castillon in 1453, England lost all its possessions on the mainland except Calais; both countries emerged from the war with a stronger sense of nationhood and with standing armies.
schwarzer-tod#summary: The plague spreads along trade routes across the whole of Europe and kills about a third of the population.
